Lighting up sustainable soft materials

We study how light drives charge and chemistry in soft materials: organic semiconductors, conducting polymers and perovskites. By combining device fabrication, home-built spectroscopy and theory, we work out where energy is lost and design better materials for solar cells, solar fuels, light detection and energy storage.

Research

Research themes

We use light to study, and improve, soft materials for clean energy. By following how charges move and react from femtoseconds to seconds, we find out where energy is lost and how to design better materials and devices.

  • Transient spectroscopy from femtoseconds to seconds
  • Photo- and spectro-electrochemistry, including operando PEC mass spectrometry
  • Materials and device fabrication, from thin films to full solar cells

Select a sector to jump to that theme

Theme 1

Organic & hybrid photovoltaics

Organic solar cells are light, flexible and printable, but they still lose too much energy as heat. We make devices from the latest materials, including hybrids with inorganic and perovskite layers, and use spectroscopy and modelling to find out where that energy goes and how to keep it.

Non-fullerene acceptorsCharge-transfer statesVoltage losses

Theme 2

Solar fuels & photoelectrochemistry

Using sunlight to split water gives clean hydrogen fuel. We build stable photoelectrodes from organic semiconductors and metal oxides, and use mass spectrometry to watch the reactions on their surface as they happen.

Water splittingHematiteOrganic photoanodesPEC-MS

Theme 3

Advanced characterisation

Many of our questions need new ways of measuring. We build and use tools that follow charges from femtoseconds to seconds, and map structure and energy down to the nanoscale.

Transient absorptionIR spectroscopyGIWAXSKPFM

Theme 4

Optoelectronics & photonics

We make light detectors that respond to only a narrow band of colours, with the selectivity built into the material itself, for health monitoring, imaging and secure communication. We are also starting work on upconversion: turning low-energy light into higher-energy light.

Narrowband photodetectorsOptical communication2D perovskitesUpconversion

Research

Our facilities

We are based in the brand-new Green Energy Hub, a £2M Faculty of Science & Engineering investment at Queen Mary's Mile End campus. Our labs take materials from solution to finished device, then measure how they work under light.

Fabrication

Device fabrication

Our device labs in the Green Energy Hub combine our own equipment with shared facilities used across SEMS and SPCS.

  • Organic semiconductor gloveboxOur own 4-glove nitrogen glovebox for organic device fabrication
  • Vacuum evaporator£450k Faculty-funded system with multi-source organic semiconductor evaporation sources
  • Perovskite gloveboxShared nitrogen glovebox for perovskite processing
  • Wet labsShared chemistry labs with fume hoods in the brand-new Green Energy Hub

Spectroscopy

Laser and optical spectroscopy

Optical labs for following excited states and charge carriers.

  • Luminescence spectroscopy (steady-state and transient)Photo- and electroluminescence on an Edinburgh Instruments FLS1000
  • In-situ FT-IR spectroscopyIncluding surface-enhanced IR (SEIRAS) and ATR, for species at surfaces and interfaces
  • Luminescence microscopyShared facility, including confocal spinning-disk imaging
  • Transient absorption spectroscopyCharge generation and recombination dynamics, from femtoseconds to seconds · through access to collaborators' facilities
  • Ultrafast IR spectroscopyTime-resolved vibrational spectroscopy of excited states and charges · through the STFC Central Laser Facility (CLF)
  • Temperature- and light-dependent J–VEnergetic landscape and voltage losses in solar cells

Photoelectrochemistry

Operando PEC-MS

Our unique photoelectrochemical mass spectrometry (PEC-MS) setup detects reaction products and intermediates in real time while a photoelectrode runs under light.

  • Illuminated EC-MS cellCustom-designed cell for measurements under light
  • PEC characterisationShared photoelectrochemical characterisation facilities

Structure & surfaces

Structural and surface analysis

Shared instruments at Queen Mary.

  • GIWAXSThin-film molecular packing and morphology · shared facility
  • KPFM and pcAFMNanoscale maps of surface potential and photocurrent · shared facility
  • UPS and XPSEnergy levels, work functions and surface chemistry · shared facility

People

The team

A growing group of experimentalists, theorists and characterisation specialists working across the energy materials stack.

Our researchers

Dr Flurin Eisner

Principal Investigator · Lecturer, SEMS

Flurin leads the group and holds a Lectureship at Queen Mary University of London. His research spans organic photovoltaics, photoelectrochemistry and soft materials for energy conversion and storage. He holds a PhD in Physics from Imperial College London, and previously held a prestigious Imperial College Research Fellowship in the Department of Materials.

Email Google Scholar ORCID QMUL profile

Dr Nathaniel Gallop

Postdoctoral Research Associate

Nathaniel joined the group in April 2026 to investigate the fundamental photophysics of solar fuels devices based on organic semiconductors, as part of Flurin's UKRI New Investigator Award. He is also a visiting senior researcher at the Leibniz Institute, and holds a PhD from Imperial College London.

Open positions

Current openings

We welcome applications from motivated researchers at all career stages, and are committed to building a diverse, inclusive and supportive team.

PhD studentship · Near-infrared light upconversion at organic semiconductor interfaces for bioimaging and optoelectronics

Develop organic materials and devices that turn near-infrared light into visible light, using interfaces between non-fullerene acceptors and annihilator molecules, for deep-tissue imaging, wearable sensors and NIR optoelectronics.

China Scholarship Council (CSC) applicants only · Tuition fees covered by Queen Mary, living costs by CSC · Starts September · Deadline 27 January 2027 · Details and how to apply

Open

PhD studentship · Waste treating waste: sunlight-driven photocatalysts from biomass residues for water remediation and solar hydrogen

Turn agricultural and food waste into low-cost photocatalysts that clean wastewater with sunlight while producing green hydrogen, tested on real wastewater in a solar flow reactor. Co-supervised with Dr Roberto Volpe.

Leverhulme Living with Waste Doctoral Programme · 4 years · Home and a limited number of international awards · Starts October 2027 · Deadline 15 January 2027 · Details and how to apply
